planting.note: Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in spring once soil has warmed, in zones 10-12 or a sheltered zone 9b site; give it full sun and generous space since mature trees grow quite large.

directions: Grow Russell like other named sapodilla selections, planting a grafted or air-layered tree in full sun on well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil in a frost-free South Florida-type landscape; established trees shrug off drought and salt wind but hard freezes below the upper 20s F cause serious damage. Selected from a seedling tree in the Florida Keys, Russell produces some of the largest fruit of any named sapodilla cultivar, nearly round, up to four inches across, with brown, scurfy skin and soft, reddish-tan, richly sweet flesh. Unlike heavier-cropping selections such as Brown Sugar or Prolific, Russell is an inconsistent bearer, so it suits growers chasing fruit size and flavor as a specimen tree rather than orchard volume. Expect several years of growth before the first crop, and harvest fruit only once the skin dulls and softens slightly, then finish ripening it at room temperature for a few days.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension - Manilkara zapota: Sapodilla (ST405)
growables.org - Tropical Fruit Cultivar Database (Sapodilla Varieties)
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil in zones 10-12; protect young trees from any temperatures near freezing.

directions: Plant grafted Modello sapodilla trees in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, using the same culture as other Manilkara zapota selections; trees are evergreen and drought-tolerant once established but suffer serious dieback below the upper 20s F. Modello bears elliptic-to-ovate fruit with light brown, moderately scurfy skin and smooth, whitish-tan flesh of good dessert quality, ripening mainly from late winter into late spring in South Florida. Yields are only fair compared with heavier-cropping cultivars like Brown Sugar or Alano, so Modello is grown more for its refined flavor and low-grit texture than for sheer volume. Harvest when the skin turns dull and scurfy and let the fruit soften at room temperature for several days before eating.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension - Manilkara zapota: Sapodilla (ST405)
growables.org - Tropical Fruit Cultivar Database (Sapodilla Varieties)
California Rare Fruit Growers

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; this dwarf selection also does well in a large container in zones cooler than 10 if overwintered indoors or in a greenhouse.

directions: Silas Woods is a naturally dwarf, compact sapodilla selection out of Homestead, Florida, staying under about 20 feet even planted in the ground, which makes it a good fit for small yards and large containers; grow it in full sun on well-drained soil and shield young trees from any freezing temperatures. Grafted trees are remarkably precocious, often producing their first fruit within one to two years of planting and cropping twice a year on roughly a six-to-eight-month cycle once mature. The round, smooth, brown-skinned fruit, two to four inches across, has a grainy, pear-like texture and a sweet, brown-sugar flavor typical of the best sapodilla selections. Because of its small stature and fast fruiting, it is one of the more practical sapodilla choices for home growers without room for a full-sized tree.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension - Manilkara zapota: Sapodilla (ST405)
Rare Fruit Council International
growables.org - Tropical Fruit Cultivar Database (Sapodilla Varieties)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10-12 or a sheltered zone 9b microclimate; hand-pollinate flowers by brush for reliable fruit set.

directions: Grow Whaley cherimoya the way you would other named Annona cherimola selections: plant a grafted tree in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and hand-pollinate the flowers with a small brush each morning, since cherimoya blossoms open female before shifting to male and rarely pollinate themselves. Dating to 1920s Hollywood, California, Whaley produces medium-to-large, elongated, conical fruit with light green, gently bumpy (tuberculate) skin and sweet, aromatic, custard-textured flesh with the classic pineapple-banana-vanilla flavor of good cherimoya. The tree tolerates cool nights better than most tropical fruit trees but is killed by hard freezes, so young plantings need winter protection in marginal zones. Grafted trees typically begin bearing within two to four years and benefit from consistent moisture through flowering and fruit set.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers - Cherimoya Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension
USDA National Plant Germplasm System

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in zones 10-12; Bays stays a manageable size, making it suited to smaller home orchards. Hand-pollinate for reliable fruit set.

directions: Bays cherimoya is grown like other named Annona cherimola selections: set out a grafted tree in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, and hand-pollinate morning-opened flowers with a small brush, since cherimoya flowers change sex through the day and rarely self-pollinate. Selected by grower James Bays in Ventura, California around 1920, this cultivar produces medium-sized, round, light green fruit marked with a distinctive fingerprint-like ('impressa') skin pattern and sweet, smooth flesh carrying the classic pineapple-banana flavor of good cherimoya. Trees are moderate growers, typically reaching only about 20 feet, which makes Bays a manageable choice for a compact home orchard compared with larger-growing selections. Protect young trees from frost and water consistently through bloom and fruit development, since cherimoya, native to cooler Andean valleys, dislikes prolonged heat and humidity nearly as much as it dislikes freezing.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers - Cherimoya Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension
USDA National Plant Germplasm System

planting.note: Plant seedlings or grafted stock in spring in deep, moist, well-drained tropical soil in full sun to light shade in frost-free zones only; this species needs both male and female trees present to fruit.

directions: Grow asam gelugur in full sun to light shade on deep, moist, well-drained tropical soil, giving it plenty of room since wild trees exceed 60 feet and even cultivated specimens become substantial shade trees over time. This dioecious species, native from the eastern Himalayas through Myanmar, Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo, and Sumatra, needs both a male and a female tree present to set fruit, producing large, round, bright orange-yellow fruit 7 to 10 centimeters across at the branch tips. The intensely sour pulp is rarely eaten fresh; instead it is sliced and sun-dried into 'asam keping,' a traditional souring ingredient used throughout Malaysian and Thai curries, fish dishes, and pickles. Give young trees consistent moisture and complete protection from cold, since the species has no frost tolerance and is strictly limited to humid, frost-free tropical gardens.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
National Parks Board Singapore - FloraFaunaWeb
Useful Tropical Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in sandy or rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in frost-free zones; this coastal species tolerates salt spray and poor soil better than true mangosteen.

directions: Seashore mangosteen thrives in the tough coastal conditions its name suggests: plant it in full sun to partial shade in sandy or rocky, well-drained soil, where it tolerates salt spray, wind, and poor soil far better than true mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana). Native to the coastal forests of Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam, it is a small to medium tree bearing smooth, beaked, pinkish-red fruit with segmented, juicy white pulp that tastes tart and citrusy with a faint banana note, milder and more sour than purple mangosteen. Botanists consider it one of the likely wild parents involved in the natural origin of true mangosteen, making it an interesting collector's tree in addition to an edible one. It has essentially no frost tolerance and needs sustained warmth and humidity, but its drought and salt tolerance make it a good option for tropical coastal gardens where G. mangostana would fail outright.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
California Rare Fruit Growers
Useful Tropical Plants Database

planting.note: Plant the whole mature fruit on its side with the stem end barely covered, exactly as with chayote, once soil is warm and all frost danger has passed.

directions: Grow tacaco exactly as you would chayote, since the two are close cucurbit relatives: plant a mature fruit on its side with the stem end barely covered in warm, rich, well-drained soil after frost danger has passed, and train the vigorous climbing vine onto a sturdy trellis or arbor. This species is essentially endemic to Costa Rica's highlands, with a small range extending into western Panama, and is almost never found outside that region, so homegrown or specialty seed stock is the main way to obtain it. The small, oval green fruit, only about three inches long, is harvested immature and boiled, giving a flavor often compared to a blend of zucchini and avocado with nutty undertones; the young shoots and leaves are eaten as greens as well. Like chayote, tacaco is a frost-tender perennial vine that resprouts from its root each year in frost-free gardens, though it remains a little-known, underexploited crop even in its home range.
sources: Useful Tropical Plants Database
CATIE (Tropical Agricultural Research and Higher Education Center, Costa Rica)
